narr: Troughing over the western CONUS brought southwesterly flow aloft over the central and northern Plains for the duration of this event. In the couple of days leading up to May 21st, the upper-level flow pattern amplified as a trough deepened over the northern Rockies. This trough then ejected out into the central Plains on the 21st. At the surface, a stationary front developed and stretched across central Nebraska and southern Iowa by the evening of the 19th. Elevated convection that morning north of the developing surface boundary resulted in isolated instances of severe hail and wind across southeast Nebraska. Additional scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed along this frontal boundary as it slowly lifted north, with a 64 miles per hour wind gust measured in Lancaster County and golf ball sized hail falling in Clarinda Iowa.||A weak low-pressure system developed the morning of the 20th in response to a shortwave rounding the base of the main trough out west, resulting in a cold front that pushed southeast across South Dakota and central Nebraska that afternoon. This front, however, stalled out across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa that evening, remaining draped across the region that night and into the morning of the 21st. Numerous rounds of strong and severe thunderstorms that night brought widespread severe weather and flash flooding, primarily across east-central Nebraska and southwest Iowa, though some elevated supercells in northeast Nebraska brought small hail to the area. After 10 UTC, an intense line of severe thunderstorms moved across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa bringing wind gusts ranging from 60 to 95 miles per hour, in addition to several spin-up tornadoes. ||As the primary upper-level disturbance ejected out over the Great Plains, intense surface cyclogenesis was noted over eastern Nebraska. This resulted in the frontal boundary that had been draped across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa that night prior to be forced northward. By 18 UTC, a strong cold front pushed through southeast Nebraska and into Iowa that afternoon. Scattered supercell thunderstorms developed along this cold front and moved across southeast Nebraska and western Iowa. These supercells became tornadic after crossing the Missouri River into Iowa, with several long-track significant tornadoes being confirmed across the state. In the OAX CWA, the strongest tornado damage confirmed was that consistent of an EF-2 in Montgomery County. This tornado continued into the DMX CWA where it caused EF-3 damage. Another tornado developed in Page County shortly before 3 PM that afternoon. This tornado went on to produce EF-4 damage in the DMX CWA. All in all, over this three-day event, 10 tornadoes were confirmed across the OAX CWA.
ev: Law Enforcement closed 276th Street north of Valley between Highway 275 and Highway 36 due to flowing water over the roadway.

Following several rounds of thunderstorms and heavy rain which resulted in flash flooding across the Omaha metro, flood waters continued to linger through the morning of the 21st. Broadcast Media reported multiple stalled vehicles at Center and 67th Street.

Several prolonged rounds of heavy rain during the early morning hours of the 21st led to flash flooding across central and northeast Saunders County. A National Weather Service employee reported water flowing over U.S. Highway 77 shortly after 7 AM, with traffic cameras showing widespread flooding across fields and roads in and around Wahoo. The Saunders County Emergency Manager also reported 6 homes flooded in Lashara, 4 of which had residents that needed to be evacuated.

The intersection of 180th and Maple was completely covered in water, with some vehicles having difficulty driving. Low-lying roads to the north of Dodge and 204th are covered with water but not all the way up to the gutters. Some cars were having trouble driving through the street. Ponding was also reported on the eastbound side of Dodge Street in Boy's Town. Further east just after 1 in the morning, two cars were reported stuck in the water in northeast Douglas County.

Several rounds of thunderstorms training over Fremont resulted in flash flooding across the city during the early morning hours of the 21st. The first report of flooding in the city came into the office at 3:47 in the morning. Just before 5 in the morning, fast-flowing water was observed over East 11th Street. Flooded roadways continued to be reported through the morning hours between Fremont and south into Saunders and northwest Douglas Counties.
The Butler County Emergency Manager reported flooding in Bruno, and in rural areas just to the south and eat of the town. Many roads were under water, particularly in the Skull Creek area.

Several rounds of thunderstorms during the early morning hours across the Omaha metro brought flash flooding to parts of the metro. The first reports of flash flooding came in just before 6:30 in the morning near Maple and 132nd Street. An additional report of flooded streets was received west of Carter Lake near the Sorensen and Fontenelle intersection. Water was also reported over a road in Boys Town.
